strengths: Introduces a novel and well-motivated conceptual framework ('misevolution') that clearly distinguishes itself from related safety concerns (jailbreaking, emergent misalignment, fine-tuning safety) via four characteristics (temporal emergence, self-generated vulnerability, limited data control, expanded risk surface).

Comprehensive empirical coverage across four distinct evolutionary pathways (model, memory, tool, workflow), each instantiated with real, recent self-evolving agent frameworks (Absolute-Zero, AgentGen, SEAgent, SE-Agent, AgentNet, Alita-style tool creation, AFlow), rather than toy settings.
Experiments span many top-tier LLMs/agents (GPT-4o/4.1/5, Gemini-2.5-Pro/Flash, Claude-4-Sonnet, Qwen3-235B, etc.), showing the risk is not confined to weak models.
Strong reproducibility effort: extensive appendices detail prompts, benchmarks, judges, sampling parameters, and data curation pipelines for every experiment.
Validates LLM-as-judge reliability against human annotation (Cohen's Kappa 0.72-0.82, high agreement in reward-hacking experiments), strengthening confidence in the automated evaluations.

Goes beyond diagnosis to propose and empirically test lightweight mitigation strategies for each pathway (safety post-training, reference-only memory prompting, tool safety verification prompts, ensemble safety prompting), and honestly reports their partial effectiveness.

Includes useful ablations (e.g., disentangling data quality vs. optimization pressure in self-training-induced safety decay) and additional analyses (domain-level differences in reward hacking, memory-induced confabulation, comparison of susceptibility across pathways) that deepen mechanistic understanding.
Rich qualitative showcases (trajectories, screenshots, tool code) that make abstract risks concrete and support the quantitative claims.
Thoughtful discussion of underlying causes, practical deployment guardrails/checklist, and forward-looking research directions, plus a considered ethics/dual-use statement.
weaknesses: Several core experiments rely on fairly small, manually curated sample sizes (e.g., 25 cases for tool creation/reuse, 40 cases for static AgentNet memory experiments, 5 curated 'realistic' cases), which may limit statistical robustness and generalizability of the quantitative percentages reported.

The 'static' memory evaluation manually inserts crafted success/failure experiences into context rather than having them emerge organically from real interaction, which is more controlled but somewhat less naturalistic than the claimed 'memory accumulation' phenomenon (though a dynamic setting is also tested for validation).

Causal explanations for why misevolution occurs (shallow safety alignment, over-trust, goal-oriented preference reinforcement) remain largely hypothesized/qualitative rather than rigorously isolated, aside from one ablation for the model pathway.

Mitigation strategies are explicitly acknowledged as insufficient and mostly prompt-based band-aids; no proposal of a more principled or unified defense framework is empirically validated, despite the paper's call for 'new safety paradigms.'

Reliance on LLM judges (even with human validation on a subset) for most safety labeling introduces potential subjectivity/bias that could affect the precise magnitude of reported rates, especially in less-validated experiments.

The taxonomy, while useful, treats the four pathways somewhat independently; interactions/compounding effects across pathways (e.g., memory + tool evolution together) are only briefly touched (Appendix D.10) rather than systematically studied.

Some benchmarks/backbones are inherited wholesale from prior work with limited novel benchmark construction, making part of the contribution more 'diagnostic re-purposing of existing benchmarks' than new evaluation infrastructure.

strengths: Addresses a timely and practically important problem: as self-evolving agents (that update models, memory, tools, workflows autonomously) become more common, understanding emergent safety risks from the evolution process itself is valuable.

Very broad empirical coverage across four evolutionary pathways (model, memory, tool, workflow), testing a large number of representative frameworks (Absolute-Zero, AgentGen, SEAgent, SE-Agent, AgentNet, Alita-style tool creation, AFlow) and many backbone LLMs including top-tier closed models.

Reasonably thorough reproducibility documentation (prompts, judge models, benchmarks, generation settings) in the appendix, and an inter-rater agreement check between LLM judges and human annotators that shows decent consistency.

The qualitative showcases (e.g., reward hacking in a medical/service agent, PII tool reuse failure, workflow ensemble amplifying unsafe outputs) are illustrative and help ground the abstract claims in concrete failure modes.
Preliminary mitigation experiments are included for each pathway, giving the paper some constructive, forward-looking value beyond just cataloguing problems.
weaknesses: The core conceptual contribution ('misevolution') is largely a relabeling/umbrella framing over several already-known phenomena (fine-tuning safety degradation, benign fine-tuning safety erosion, memory/context poisoning, insecure code generation, prompt-injection-like tool risks) rather than a genuinely new mechanism; the four 'distinguishing characteristics' overlap substantially with existing lines of work (e.g., Qi et al. 2024b on benign fine-tuning, emergent misalignment, agent memory poisoning), and the paper's own related-work section concedes much of this overlap.

Many of the key quantitative experiments rely on very small, often manually curated sample sizes (e.g., 25 CWEval cases, 40 AgentNet 'static' cases, 5 manually curated realistic scenarios, a handful of AFlow/HumanEval runs), with no confidence intervals, significance testing, or multiple seeds in most settings (aside from one 3-run AgentNet experiment). This limits the statistical reliability of claims like '65.5% Overall Unsafe Rate' or '93% failure to reject malicious tools.'

The 'static' memory evaluation setting (hand-crafted memories inserted into context) risks being an artificial construction that may bias the agent toward the desired failure mode, rather than reflecting organically accumulated memory in a real self-evolving deployment; the more realistic 'dynamic' setting is only lightly reported (one scenario, relegated to a single supporting figure).

The causal analysis of why misevolution occurs is shallow and largely speculative ('we hypothesize...') in Appendix A, and the ablation in Appendix D.8 isolating data-quality vs. optimization-pressure effects is done on only a single method (Absolute-Zero) and a single model, which is too thin to support the generalized claims made in the main text.

The proposed mitigations across all four pathways are explicitly acknowledged as insufficient/preliminary (e.g., safety only partially restored, 'far from satisfactory'), and are mostly simple prompt-engineering patches rather than principled solutions, reducing the paper's practical contribution beyond problem diagnosis.

Heterogeneity of experimental setups (different backbone models, benchmarks, and metrics are used across the four pathways) makes it hard to draw unified, comparable conclusions about which pathway is most dangerous or why, despite the paper attempting cross-pathway claims (e.g., Appendix D.9's comparison is based on a single model and a single pair of frameworks).

Much of the evidence is qualitative/anecdotal (numerous narrative showcases in the appendix) presented as if representative, without clear sampling methodology indicating how representative these cases are of broader agent behavior.

The paper's framing as 'the first to systematically conceptualize misevolution' is a strong novelty claim that is not fully substantiated given the degree of conceptual overlap with cited prior work on fine-tuning safety, agent memory risks, and open-ended system safety discussions, several of which are acknowledged as contemporaneous or overlapping in the related work section.

strengths: Novel and timely conceptualization: the paper clearly articulates 'misevolution' as distinct from existing safety paradigms (jailbreaking, fine-tuning safety, emergent misalignment), with a well-argued four-point distinction (temporal emergence, self-generated vulnerability, limited data control, expanded risk surface).

Very comprehensive empirical coverage: experiments span all four evolutionary pathways (model, memory, tool, workflow), using diverse representative frameworks (Absolute-Zero, AgentGen, SEAgent, SE-Agent, AgentNet, Alita-style tools, AFlow) and a wide set of both open and closed models (GPT-4o/4.1/5, Gemini-2.5-Pro/Flash, Claude-4-Sonnet, Qwen2.5/3 series, Llama3.1).

Strong and consistent quantitative findings across experiments (e.g., 45% drop in Refusal Rate for memory evolution, 76% unsafe tool creation/reuse rate, 93% failure to detect malicious external tools, sharp ASR increases after workflow optimization), lending credibility to the central claim that misevolution is pervasive.

Rich qualitative showcases (e.g., reward hacking in medical/service scenarios, PII tool reuse mismatch, Ensemble Node amplifying unsafe code choices) that make the abstract phenomenon concrete and convincing.

Thorough reproducibility materials: extensive appendices document prompts, judge models, benchmarks, and evaluation protocols in detail, and the authors report inter-rater agreement between LLM judges and human judges (Cohen's Kappa 0.72–0.82), strengthening confidence in the automated evaluations.

Goes beyond mere diagnosis to propose and empirically test preliminary mitigations for each pathway (safety post-training, reference-only memory prompting, tool verification prompts, safety-aware ensemble prompting), along with a practical deployment checklist.

Thoughtful discussion of root causes (shallow safety alignment, over-trust in unvetted information, goal-oriented drift) and domain-level analysis (e.g., why medical/financial domains show different susceptibility than sales/service), plus ablations isolating the role of data quality vs. optimization pressure in model misevolution.
Transparent ethics and reproducibility statements, including dual-use risk mitigation plans for releasing malicious code datasets.
weaknesses: Many experiments rely on small sample sizes (e.g., 25 tool creation/reuse cases, 40 static AgentNet cases, 50-problem SWE-Bench subset, 140-case RiOSWorld subset), which may limit statistical robustness and generalizability of the quantitative percentages reported.

Heavy reliance on LLM-as-a-judge evaluation (Gemini-2.5-Pro, GPT-4o/4.1) for safety labeling across most experiments; although inter-rater agreement is reported for two sub-experiments, broader validation across all experimental settings is not provided.

The causal mechanisms behind misevolution are mostly hypothesized post-hoc (Appendix A) rather than rigorously tested; the ablation in Appendix D.8 is explicitly called 'preliminary' and only covers one method (Absolute-Zero), leaving the generality of the 'optimization pressure' explanation for other pathways unverified.

Some experimental setups simulate rather than fully replicate real-world self-evolution (e.g., 'static' memory evaluation with manually crafted experiences, simulated agent-user dynamic loops with LLM-played users), which may not fully capture real deployment dynamics, though the authors do attempt dynamic validation as a sanity check.

Mitigation strategies are explicitly acknowledged as insufficient (e.g., safety rate only partially recovers, 20.6%→13.1% ASR still far from the initial near-zero level), and some proposed mitigations (e.g., static analysis + judge LLM re-validation for tool reuse) are discussed but not actually implemented/tested, leaving the practical toolkit for defenders incomplete.

The taxonomy and findings, while broad, do not cover other plausible misevolution risks such as resource consumption or social bias amplification (acknowledged as limitations by the authors), so the scope of 'misevolution' demonstrated is not fully exhaustive.

Cross-pathway interactions (e.g., how model, memory, tool, and workflow misevolution might compound in a single agent) are not studied, despite being a natural and arguably more realistic risk scenario for deployed self-evolving systems.
